planting.note: Set plugs or bare-root crowns into raised, well-drained beds in October in zone 9a Gulf Coast gardens for a winter-into-spring harvest; because it is day-neutral it will keep setting fruit through warm weather rather than stopping after one spring flush, so plan on steady picking rather than a single concentrated peak.

directions: Royal Royce is a day-neutral cultivar from the University of California, Davis strawberry breeding program that largely displaced older varieties on California's central coast within a few seasons of its release because of its heavy, consistent fruiting and firm, glossy fruit. Grow it exactly as you would any modern plasticulture strawberry, with drip irrigation under black plastic and regular fertigation to keep up with its near-continuous bloom and fruit set. Along the Gulf Coast it performs well as a fall-planted annual, cropping from late winter through spring before heat shuts it down for the season. Remove runners promptly to channel energy into fruit rather than daughter plants, since day-neutral types produce far fewer runners than June bearers but still benefit from the practice.
sources: University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources
LSU AgCenter — Strawberry Variety Evaluation for Louisiana

planting.note: Plant dormant crowns or plugs in fall in mild-winter zones such as 9a for a winter and spring crop; this day-neutral selection from the UC Davis breeding program was developed with export shipping in mind, so it rewards the same raised-bed, drip-irrigated culture used for commercial plasticulture strawberries.

directions: Rosa Linda is a day-neutral strawberry out of the University of California, Davis program, bred with an emphasis on fruit firmness so berries could travel long distances for export markets. The berries are medium-sized, well-colored, and hold up noticeably better after picking than softer-fleshed heirloom types, making it a good choice for home growers who want to hold a harvest a few extra days before eating or preserving it. Give it the same fertile, well-drained, full-sun bed as other modern cultivars and keep irrigation consistent, since uneven watering shows up quickly as misshapen or doubled fruit. Expect flushes of production spread across the cool season in zone 9a rather than one single heavy peak.
sources: University of California Division of Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root crowns in late winter to early spring with the crown held right at soil level; pinch off any flowers that form the first season so plants build a strong matted row and fruit heavily the following year.

directions: Blakemore was released by USDA breeders in 1929 and for several decades afterward was the backbone short-day cultivar of commercial strawberry production across the South and Mid-Atlantic, prized for ripening early and for berries firm enough to survive shipping in an era before refrigerated trucking was common. The fruit is small to medium, conical, and bright red, with a tart edge that makes it better suited to preserves and shortcake than fresh eating straight off the vine by modern sweetness standards. It is a vigorous runner-producing June bearer that fills a matted row quickly, and its parentage runs through many later Southern-adapted varieties bred to improve on its flavor while keeping its hardiness and early ripening. Grow it as a heritage or historical-interest planting in a sunny, well-drained bed, watching for the leaf spot and virus susceptibility that eventually pushed commercial growers toward newer releases.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in late winter to early spring in a sunny, well-drained matted-row bed; this early-20th-century heirloom was grown commercially as a winter-truck crop in the Gulf South and still suits the same mild-winter planting window today.

directions: Missionary was one of the leading commercial strawberry varieties grown across the Gulf South in the early twentieth century, including in the once-famous Louisiana strawberry districts around Hammond, before firmer-fruited releases such as Blakemore largely replaced it in the 1930s. It is a June-bearing heirloom with soft, aromatic, deep red berries that were valued more for flavor than for shipping toughness, which is exactly why home gardeners seeking old-fashioned strawberry taste still seek it out today. Because the fruit bruises and softens quickly after picking, plan to eat or preserve it within a day or two of harvest rather than storing it. Give it a fertile, well-drained bed in full sun and divide the matted row every few years to keep the planting vigorous, since this variety predates modern disease-resistance breeding and can decline where strawberry diseases build up in the soil.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Strawberry Variety Evaluation for Louisiana

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in late winter to early spring with the crown level at the soil surface, and remove the first season's flowers so the planting builds a dense matted row before its first full crop.

directions: Pocahontas is a mid-twentieth-century USDA release from the same breeding lineage that produced Blakemore, developed to keep that variety's hardiness and early ripening while improving berry size and yield for growers across the Mid-Atlantic and upper South. It is a vigorous June bearer that throws runners freely and fills a matted row quickly, producing large, firm, bright red conical berries with a brisk, old-fashioned flavor well suited to preserving as well as fresh eating. Plant it in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and renovate the bed every two to three years by mowing foliage and thinning runners, which keeps older plantings of this heirloom productive far longer than letting the row crowd itself out. It is a useful variety for gardeners who want historic Southern strawberry stock with somewhat sturdier fruit than earlier releases like Blakemore or Missionary.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Set dormant bare-root crowns in late winter to early spring in a sunny, well-drained matted-row bed, spacing plants generously since this old Southern variety runners aggressively and fills in faster than most modern cultivars.

directions: Albritton is a mid-twentieth-century Southern heirloom strawberry remembered chiefly for its extraordinary vigor and heavy yield, out-producing many of the shipping varieties of its era in home garden and local-market trials. The trade-off for that productivity is fruit that softens quickly after ripening, so it suits growers who sell or eat berries close to home rather than those needing a few days of shelf life. Expect an exceptionally vigorous matted row that needs more aggressive runner thinning and bed renovation than modern, more restrained cultivars to avoid overcrowding and declining berry size. Grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil as a flavorful, high-yielding curiosity for gardeners interested in Southern strawberry history rather than as a shipping crop.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Set dormant crowns in late winter to early spring with the crown level at the soil surface; this late-blooming mid-South heirloom dodges many late frosts that nip earlier-flowering varieties, a useful trait in gardens with unpredictable spring cold snaps.

directions: Tennessee Beauty is a mid-twentieth-century heirloom June bearer that was a mainstay of home gardens and local markets across Tennessee and the mid-South, prized for its sweet, old-fashioned flavor and for blooming later than many other varieties of its era, which helped it escape frost damage to spring blossoms. The berries are medium-sized, glossy, and deep red, with a classic strawberry aroma that many gardeners who remember it describe as superior to modern, firmer-fleshed shipping varieties. Grow it in full sun in a fertile, well-drained matted-row bed and divide crowded rows every few years, since like most heirlooms it was never bred for the disease resistance found in current commercial releases. It makes a good companion planting to an early-season variety for gardeners wanting to stretch the harvest window using only historic Southern cultivars.
sources: North Carolina State University Cooperative Extension
